summary: A BBN note on software checksumming added to the IMP and TIP programs to improve network reliability. The designers had first assumed only communication circuits were error-prone, then added checks for errors in other parts, and advise host staff to note two sections that may need changes in their procedures.

plainLanguage.summary: The network's box makers added extra self-checks, because broken parts, not just wires, could scramble messages.

questions: why did arpanet add software checksums
what hardware errors did software checksums detect
how did arpanet protect routing messages
subtitle: Detecting errors hidden inside the network switches themselves.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET had assumed only communication wires could fail, but experience showed hardware inside the switches (IMPs) corrupts data too. When a switch's memory or processor failed, it could scramble messages and routing information, breaking the entire network.
tldr.mechanism: Software checksums were added to every packet as it travels from switch to switch, and routing messages now verify themselves as they are built. If a packet arrives corrupted, the receiver discards it and the sender retransmits.
tldr.outcome: The team detected and fixed modem and memory failures at multiple sites, and the technique became a permanent part of the IMP system. Future hardware was designed with a dedicated checksum generator.

facts.label: Checksum method
facts.value: Simple sum of words plus word count

today: RFC 528 describes experimental reliability improvements deployed in 1973. These software checksumming techniques became permanent features of the IMP system and influenced the design of all subsequent ARPANET components.

sections.title: Network Reliability and Hardware Failures
sections.content:
The ARPA network's designers originally believed that only communications circuits could fail and cause errors. The modems on each IMP had a hardware checksum to protect against transmission errors. In practice, experience revealed that hardware failures inside the IMPs themselves—memory errors, processor faults, and modem interface problems—could silently corrupt data in ways that looked like lost or corrupted messages.

One notable incident in 1971 involved the Harvard IMP's faulty memory, which caused it to broadcast routing messages saying it had zero delay to all destinations. This false routing information spread through the network, making most traffic fail. Software checksums on routing messages stopped this kind of cascading failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The switches were breaking in weird ways that broke the whole network. One switch had a bad memory chip that told everyone it was the best route to everywhere, and nobody noticed until mail got scrambled all over the country.

sections.title: End-to-End Packet Checksums
sections.content:
The IMP software now calculates a checksum on each packet when it arrives from the source host. At each intermediate switch, the checksum is verified as the packet arrives. If the packet is corrupted, it is discarded and the previous switch retransmits it (since it receives no acknowledgment). The first switch only verifies the checksum on retransmission, which cuts the number of checks in half. Once a packet successfully reaches the destination switch, the checksum is verified one last time before the packet is delivered to the host.

This technique provides continuous end-to-end protection with no gaps where the packet could be corrupted undetected. Any errors are reported to the Network Control Center with a copy of the corrupted packet for diagnosis. The checksum adds little overhead: on a 516 IMP, the processor bandwidth drops by about 12.5 percent, from one megabit per second to 875 kilobits per second.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package gets a seal code added at the start. Every mail sorter checks the code when it arrives and the next sorter checks it again. If the code looks wrong, the package is sent back.

sections.title: Protecting Routing Information
sections.content:
Corrupted routing messages are even more dangerous than corrupted data packets because one bad routing decision affects all traffic. The routing program was modified to build its own software checksum as it constructs the routing message, rather than reading what was stored in memory. The sending process always verifies this checksum before transmitting. Additionally, the routing program code itself is checksummed; processes that execute routing code first verify the code has not been corrupted. If the code checksum fails, the IMP requests a fresh copy from a neighboring switch before continuing.

A broken instruction in one IMP's routing program once caused it to send pure random data as routing updates, paralyzing the network until the machine was shut down. Self-verifying routing protects against this class of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The map that tells each sorter where to send packages is checked twice: once while it is being written, and again before it is used. If the map looks broken, it gets reloaded from a neighbor.

sections.title: Rollout and Future Plans
sections.content:
The packet checksum code was released on June 19, 1973, after the team uncovered hardware problems with modem interfaces and memory at multiple sites. These same errors—a modem dropping bits, another picking up bits, a third dropping words—would have been nearly impossible to diagnose without the software checksum data. The routing checksum was released earlier, on May 22.

Future IMP designs will include dedicated hardware for checksum generation and verification, making the checks faster and more comprehensive. The team also plans an optional checksum between each host and the network, completing the chain so that two hosts can be certain of error-free delivery or be notified of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: They turned on the new checks in the real network and found broken parts right away. Future mail stations will have a special machine that checks codes super fast.

references.text: McQuillan, J. M., Walden, D. C., "The ARPA Network Design Decisions", ACM Computer Communication Review, vol. 4, no. 1, April 1974.
